Assertion rewriting issue with editable-installed plugins

### Problem

When I look into/debug external plugins, my workflow is:

- Create a venv
- Run `pip install -e .` (this is with a recent pip and setuptools backend, so is using "new style" [PEP 660](https://peps.python.org/pep-0660/) editable installs. `editable_mode=strict` doesn't seem to make a difference)
- Run `pytest`

While doing this for several plugins recently (e.g. pytest-asyncio), I've noticed pytest issues a warning:

```
../../../../home/ran/src/pytest/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py:759
  /home/ran/src/pytest/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py:759: PytestAssertRewriteWarning: Module already imported so cannot be rewritten: pytest_asyncio
    self.import_plugin(import_spec)
```

### Analysis

This is my understanding of why this happens:

- pytest's assertion rewriting requires that a module be marked for rewrite before it is imported.
- For external plugins this is done by the [_mark_plugins_for_rewrite](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/blob/13eacdad8ac434b4336cf1e6496869815a6457c7/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py#L1211) function.
- This function iterates over all files of all installed distributions which have a `pytest11` entry point, and marks their modules for rewrite if necessary.

This ends up now working with my workflow because the `distribution.files` doesn't contain any of the actual package python files. Relevant issues: https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/96144 https://github.com/pypa/packaging-problems/issues/620

Currently there is no solution from the packaging side. It might be possible to add a workaround on the pytest side, I'm not sure.
description:
## Problem

`_mark_plugins_for_rewrite()` decides which modules to mark for assertion rewriting by walking the Python files recorded in each plugin distribution's metadata. A PEP 660 editable install doesn't record them — `dist.files` only holds the `__editable__*.pth` shim and the `dist-info` entries — so nothing matches and the plugin never gets marked.

The effect is that assertions inside a plugin stop being rewritten as soon as it is installed with `pip install -e .`, which is the usual way to work on one. With a plugin that asserts in its own helpers:

```python
# myplug/helper.py
def compare(got, want):
    assert got == want
```

```
# pip install .
E       AssertionError: assert {'a': 1, 'b': 2} == {'a': 1, 'b': 3}

# pip install -e .
E       AssertionError
```

## Fix

When a distribution is installed in editable mode and its recorded files yield no rewritable module, fall back to the top-level package of its `pytest11` entry points. Editable mode is read from `direct_url.json` (PEP 610), so regular installs keep taking the existing file-based path untouched.

The `direct_url.json` gate matters. Without it the fallback also fires for distributions that simply record no files, which a number of tests in the suite construct, and 13 of them change behaviour.

## Tests

The new test covers three distributions: an editable one, a regular install from a local directory, and one installed from an index with no `direct_url.json`. Only the editable case fails on `main`.

Fixes #11783

Assertion rewriting issue with editable-installed plugins

### Problem

When I look into/debug external plugins, my workflow is:

- Create a venv
- Run `pip install -e .` (this is with a recent pip and setuptools backend, so is using "new style" [PEP 660](https://peps.python.org/pep-0660/) editable installs. `editable_mode=strict` doesn't seem to make a difference)
- Run `pytest`

While doing this for several plugins recently (e.g. pytest-asyncio), I've noticed pytest issues a warning:

```
../../../../home/ran/src/pytest/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py:759
  /home/ran/src/pytest/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py:759: PytestAssertRewriteWarning: Module already imported so cannot be rewritten: pytest_asyncio
    self.import_plugin(import_spec)
```

### Analysis

This is my understanding of why this happens:

- pytest's assertion rewriting requires that a module be marked for rewrite before it is imported.
- For external plugins this is done by the [_mark_plugins_for_rewrite](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/blob/13eacdad8ac434b4336cf1e6496869815a6457c7/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py#L1211) function.
- This function iterates over all files of all installed distributions which have a `pytest11` entry point, and marks their modules for rewrite if necessary.

This ends up now working with my workflow because the `distribution.files` doesn't contain any of the actual package python files. Relevant issues: https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/96144 https://github.com/pypa/packaging-problems/issues/620

Currently there is no solution from the packaging side. It might be possible to add a workaround on the pytest side, I'm not sure.
description:
## Problem

`_mark_plugins_for_rewrite()` decides which modules to mark for assertion rewriting by walking the Python files recorded in each plugin distribution's metadata. A PEP 660 editable install doesn't record them — `dist.files` only holds the `__editable__*.pth` shim and the `dist-info` entries — so nothing matches and the plugin never gets marked.

The effect is that assertions inside a plugin stop being rewritten as soon as it is installed with `pip install -e .`, which is the usual way to work on one. With a plugin that asserts in its own helpers:

```python
# myplug/helper.py
def compare(got, want):
    assert got == want
```

```
# pip install .
E       AssertionError: assert {'a': 1, 'b': 2} == {'a': 1, 'b': 3}

# pip install -e .
E       AssertionError
```

## Fix

When a distribution is installed in editable mode and its recorded files yield no rewritable module, fall back to the top-level package of its `pytest11` entry points. Editable mode is read from `direct_url.json` (PEP 610), so regular installs keep taking the existing file-based path untouched.

The `direct_url.json` gate matters. Without it the fallback also fires for distributions that simply record no files, which a number of tests in the suite construct, and 13 of them change behaviour.

## Tests

The new test covers three distributions: an editable one, a regular install from a local directory, and one installed from an index with no `direct_url.json`. Only the editable case fails on `main`.

Fixes #11783

Assertion rewriting issue with editable-installed plugins

### Problem

When I look into/debug external plugins, my workflow is:

- Create a venv
- Run `pip install -e .` (this is with a recent pip and setuptools backend, so is using "new style" [PEP 660](https://peps.python.org/pep-0660/) editable installs. `editable_mode=strict` doesn't seem to make a difference)
- Run `pytest`

While doing this for several plugins recently (e.g. pytest-asyncio), I've noticed pytest issues a warning:

```
../../../../home/ran/src/pytest/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py:759
  /home/ran/src/pytest/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py:759: PytestAssertRewriteWarning: Module already imported so cannot be rewritten: pytest_asyncio
    self.import_plugin(import_spec)
```

### Analysis

This is my understanding of why this happens:

- pytest's assertion rewriting requires that a module be marked for rewrite before it is imported.
- For external plugins this is done by the [_mark_plugins_for_rewrite](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/blob/13eacdad8ac434b4336cf1e6496869815a6457c7/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py#L1211) function.
- This function iterates over all files of all installed distributions which have a `pytest11` entry point, and marks their modules for rewrite if necessary.

This ends up now working with my workflow because the `distribution.files` doesn't contain any of the actual package python files. Relevant issues: https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/96144 https://github.com/pypa/packaging-problems/issues/620

Currently there is no solution from the packaging side. It might be possible to add a workaround on the pytest side, I'm not sure.

description:
## Problem

`_mark_plugins_for_rewrite()` decides which modules to mark for assertion rewriting by walking the Python files recorded in each plugin distribution's metadata. A PEP 660 editable install doesn't record them — `dist.files` only holds the `__editable__*.pth` shim and the `dist-info` entries — so nothing matches and the plugin never gets marked.

The effect is that assertions inside a plugin stop being rewritten as soon as it is installed with `pip install -e .`, which is the usual way to work on one. With a plugin that asserts in its own helpers:

```python
# myplug/helper.py
def compare(got, want):
    assert got == want
```

```
# pip install .
E       AssertionError: assert {'a': 1, 'b': 2} == {'a': 1, 'b': 3}

# pip install -e .
E       AssertionError
```

## Fix

When a distribution is installed in editable mode and its recorded files yield no rewritable module, fall back to the top-level package of its `pytest11` entry points. Editable mode is read from `direct_url.json` (PEP 610), so regular installs keep taking the existing file-based path untouched.

The `direct_url.json` gate matters. Without it the fallback also fires for distributions that simply record no files, which a number of tests in the suite construct, and 13 of them change behaviour.

## Tests

The new test covers three distributions: an editable one, a regular install from a local directory, and one installed from an index with no `direct_url.json`. Only the editable case fails on `main`.

Fixes #11783

Assertion rewriting issue with editable-installed plugins

### Problem

When I look into/debug external plugins, my workflow is:

- Create a venv
- Run `pip install -e .` (this is with a recent pip and setuptools backend, so is using "new style" [PEP 660](https://peps.python.org/pep-0660/) editable installs. `editable_mode=strict` doesn't seem to make a difference)
- Run `pytest`

While doing this for several plugins recently (e.g. pytest-asyncio), I've noticed pytest issues a warning:

```
../../../../home/ran/src/pytest/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py:759
  /home/ran/src/pytest/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py:759: PytestAssertRewriteWarning: Module already imported so cannot be rewritten: pytest_asyncio
    self.import_plugin(import_spec)
```

### Analysis

This is my understanding of why this happens:

- pytest's assertion rewriting requires that a module be marked for rewrite before it is imported.
- For external plugins this is done by the [_mark_plugins_for_rewrite](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/blob/13eacdad8ac434b4336cf1e6496869815a6457c7/src/_pytest/config/__init__.py#L1211) function.
- This function iterates over all files of all installed distributions which have a `pytest11` entry point, and marks their modules for rewrite if necessary.

This ends up now working with my workflow because the `distribution.files` doesn't contain any of the actual package python files. Relevant issues: https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/96144 https://github.com/pypa/packaging-problems/issues/620

Currently there is no solution from the packaging side. It might be possible to add a workaround on the pytest side, I'm not sure.
description:
## Problem

`_mark_plugins_for_rewrite()` decides which modules to mark for assertion rewriting by walking the Python files recorded in each plugin distribution's metadata. A PEP 660 editable install doesn't record them — `dist.files` only holds the `__editable__*.pth` shim and the `dist-info` entries — so nothing matches and the plugin never gets marked.

The effect is that assertions inside a plugin stop being rewritten as soon as it is installed with `pip install -e .`, which is the usual way to work on one. With a plugin that asserts in its own helpers:

```python
# myplug/helper.py
def compare(got, want):
    assert got == want
```

```
# pip install .
E       AssertionError: assert {'a': 1, 'b': 2} == {'a': 1, 'b': 3}

# pip install -e .
E       AssertionError
```

## Fix

When a distribution is installed in editable mode and its recorded files yield no rewritable module, fall back to the top-level package of its `pytest11` entry points. Editable mode is read from `direct_url.json` (PEP 610), so regular installs keep taking the existing file-based path untouched.

The `direct_url.json` gate matters. Without it the fallback also fires for distributions that simply record no files, which a number of tests in the suite construct, and 13 of them change behaviour.

## Tests

The new test covers three distributions: an editable one, a regular install from a local directory, and one installed from an index with no `direct_url.json`. Only the editable case fails on `main`.

Fixes #11783

_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. An int `0` (NOTSET) still counts as set, matching the old `"0"` string. The `int | bool | str` order for `log_auto_indent` keeps ini `"1"` meaning one space, not `True`.

**Compat note:** because union members are tried in order, `getini()` now returns `int` for ini-file values like `verbosity_assertions = 2` or `log_level = 10`, where it used to return a `str`. This is the same trade-off #14954 made for `max_warnings`. Callers in pytest already convert with `int()`. A third-party plugin that calls `getini()` on these options and expects a `str` would see the change.

**Docs:** the "must be quoted in TOML" notes are removed. The TOML `minversion = 3.0` example is now quoted, because a float is rejected there and would turn `8.10` into `8.1`. Copy-pasted `log_cli_level` lines in the `log_level` and `log_file_level` examples are fixed, and the `--help` dump is refreshed (it also had a stale `faulthandler_timeout`).

- [x] If AI agents were used, they are credited in `Co-authored-by` commit trailers.

_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. An int `0` (NOTSET) still counts as set, matching the old `"0"` string. The `int | bool | str` order for `log_auto_indent` keeps ini `"1"` meaning one space, not `True`.

**Compat note:** because union members are tried in order, `getini()` now returns `int` for ini-file values like `verbosity_assertions = 2` or `log_level = 10`, where it used to return a `str`. This is the same trade-off #14954 made for `max_warnings`. Callers in pytest already convert with `int()`. A third-party plugin that calls `getini()` on these options and expects a `str` would see the change.

**Docs:** the "must be quoted in TOML" notes are removed. The TOML `minversion = 3.0` example is now quoted, because a float is rejected there and would turn `8.10` into `8.1`. Copy-pasted `log_cli_level` lines in the `log_level` and `log_file_level` examples are fixed, and the `--help` dump is refreshed (it also had a stale `faulthandler_timeout`).

    """A logging formatter which formats record with
    :func:`datetime.datetime.strftime` formatter instead of
    :func:`time.strftime` in case of microseconds in format string.
    """

    def formatTime(self, record: LogRecord, datefmt: str | None = None) -> str:
        if datefmt and "%f" in datefmt:
            ct = self.converter(record.created)
            tz = timezone(timedelta(seconds=ct.tm_gmtoff), ct.tm_zone)
            # Construct `datetime.datetime` object from `struct_time`
            # and msecs information from `record`

        return super().formatTime(record, datefmt)

Accept native TOML types for the remaining built-in ini options

<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"RonnyPfannschmidt"} -->
_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. An int `0` (NOTSET) still counts as set, matching the old `"0"` string. The `int | bool | str` order for `log_auto_indent` keeps ini `"1"` meaning one space, not `True`.

**Compat note:** because union members are tried in order, `getini()` now returns `int` for ini-file values like `verbosity_assertions = 2` or `log_level = 10`, where it used to return a `str`. This is the same trade-off #14954 made for `max_warnings`. Callers in pytest already convert with `int()`. A third-party plugin that calls `getini()` on these options and expects a `str` would see the change.

**Docs:** the "must be quoted in TOML" notes are removed. The TOML `minversion = 3.0` example is now quoted, because a float is rejected there and would turn `8.10` into `8.1`. Copy-pasted `log_cli_level` lines in the `log_level` and `log_file_level` examples are fixed, and the `--help` dump is refreshed (it also had a stale `faulthandler_timeout`).

- [x] If AI agents were used, they are credited in `Co-authored-by` commit trailers.

_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. An int `0` (NOTSET) still counts as set, matching the old `"0"` string. The `int | bool | str` order for `log_auto_indent` keeps ini `"1"` meaning one space, not `True`.

**Compat note:** because union members are tried in order, `getini()` now returns `int` for ini-file values like `verbosity_assertions = 2` or `log_level = 10`, where it used to return a `str`. This is the same trade-off #14954 made for `max_warnings`. Callers in pytest already convert with `int()`. A third-party plugin that calls `getini()` on these options and expects a `str` would see the change.

**Docs:** the "must be quoted in TOML" notes are removed. The TOML `minversion = 3.0` example is now quoted, because a float is rejected there and would turn `8.10` into `8.1`. Copy-pasted `log_cli_level` lines in the `log_level` and `log_file_level` examples are fixed, and the `--help` dump is refreshed (it also had a stale `faulthandler_timeout`).

    :func:`time.strftime` in case of microseconds in format string.

    def formatTime(self, record: LogRecord, datefmt: str | None = None) -> str:
        if datefmt and "%f" in datefmt:
            ct = self.converter(record.created)
            tz = timezone(timedelta(seconds=ct.tm_gmtoff), ct.tm_zone)
            # Construct `datetime.datetime` object from `struct_time`
            # and msecs information from `record`
            # Using int() instead of round() to avoid it exceeding 1_000_000 and causing a ValueError (#11861).

Accept native TOML types for the remaining built-in ini options

<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"RonnyPfannschmidt"} -->
_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. An int `0` (NOTSET) still counts as set, matching the old `"0"` string. The `int | bool | str` order for `log_auto_indent` keeps ini `"1"` meaning one space, not `True`.

**Compat note:** because union members are tried in order, `getini()` now returns `int` for ini-file values like `verbosity_assertions = 2` or `log_level = 10`, where it used to return a `str`. This is the same trade-off #14954 made for `max_warnings`. Callers in pytest already convert with `int()`. A third-party plugin that calls `getini()` on these options and expects a `str` would see the change.

**Docs:** the "must be quoted in TOML" notes are removed. The TOML `minversion = 3.0` example is now quoted, because a float is rejected there and would turn `8.10` into `8.1`. Copy-pasted `log_cli_level` lines in the `log_level` and `log_file_level` examples are fixed, and the `--help` dump is refreshed (it also had a stale `faulthandler_timeout`).

- [x] Include new tests or update existing tests when applicable.
- [x] Allow maintainers to push and squash when merging my commits.
- [x] If AI agents were used, they are credited in `Co-authored-by` commit trailers.
- [x] Create a new changelog file in the `changelog` directory.

Accept native TOML types for the remaining built-in ini options

<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"RonnyPfannschmidt"} -->
_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. Accept native TOML types for the remaining built-in ini options

<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"RonnyPfannschmidt"} -->
_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. An int `0` (NOTSET) still counts as set, matching the old `"0"` string. The `int | bool | str` order for `log_auto_indent` keeps ini `"1"` meaning one space, not `True`.

**Compat note:** because union members are tried in order, `getini()` now returns `int` for ini-file values like `verbosity_assertions = 2` or `log_level = 10`, where it used to return a `str`. This is the same trade-off #14954 made for `max_warnings`. Callers in pytest already convert with `int()`. A third-party plugin that calls `getini()` on these options and expects a `str` would see the change.

**Docs:** the "must be quoted in TOML" notes are removed. The TOML `minversion = 3.0` example is now quoted, because a float is rejected there and would turn `8.10` into `8.1`. Copy-pasted `log_cli_level` lines in the `log_level` and `log_file_level` examples are fixed, and the `--help` dump is refreshed (it also had a stale `faulthandler_timeout`).

Accept native TOML types for the remaining built-in ini options

<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"RonnyPfannschmidt"} -->
_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. An int `0` (NOTSET) still counts as set, matching the old `"0"` string. The `int | bool | str` order for `log_auto_indent` keeps ini `"1"` meaning one space, not `True`.

**Compat note:** because union members are tried in order, `getini()` now returns `int` for ini-file values like `verbosity_assertions = 2` or `log_level = 10`, where it used to return a `str`. This is the same trade-off #14954 made for `max_warnings`. Callers in pytest already convert with `int()`. A third-party plugin that calls `getini()` on these options and expects a `str` would see the change.

**Docs:** the "must be quoted in TOML" notes are removed. The TOML `minversion = 3.0` example is now quoted, because a float is rejected there and would turn `8.10` into `8.1`. Copy-pasted `log_cli_level` lines in the `log_level` and `log_file_level` examples are fixed, and the `--help` dump is refreshed (it also had a stale `faulthandler_timeout`).

- [x] Allow maintainers to push and squash when merging my commits.
- [x] If AI agents were used, they are credited in `Co-authored-by` commit trailers.

class DatetimeFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    """A logging formatter which formats record with
    :func:`datetime.datetime.strftime` formatter instead of
    :func:`time.strftime` in case of microseconds in format string.
    """

    def formatTime(self, record: LogRecord, datefmt: str | None = None) -> str:
        if datefmt and "%f" in datefmt:
            ct = self.converter(record.created)
            tz = timezone(timedelta(seconds=ct.tm_gmtoff), ct.tm_zone)
            # Construct `datetime.datetime` object from `struct_time`
            # and msecs information from `record`
            # Using int() instead of round() to avoid it exceeding 1_000_000 and causing a ValueError (#11861).
            dt = datetime(*ct[0:6], microsecond=int(record.msecs * 1000), tzinfo=tz)
            return dt.strftime(datefmt)
        # Use `logging.Formatter` for non-microsecond formats
        return super().formatTime(record, datefmt)

Accept native TOML types for the remaining built-in ini options

<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"RonnyPfannschmidt"} -->
_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR324YsGieeNgCDmzWvRNaki)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #14692, #14954 and #15133. This finishes the job for every built-in option whose value is naturally a number, a boolean or a fixed choice.

**Before:** in a native `pytest.toml` / `[tool.pytest]` config, `verbosity_assertions = 2`, `tmp_path_retention_count = 3`, `log_level = 10` or `log_auto_indent = true` failed with "expects a string, got int/bool", and the docs told users to quote them. `log_file_mode = "x"` crashed with an INTERNALERROR, and an unknown `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` was only caught when a long id was generated.

**After:** these values are accepted unquoted. Quoted strings and ini files keep working. Invalid choices are reported as a `UsageError` when the option is read.

| option | new type |
|---|---|
| `verbosity_assertions`, `verbosity_test_cases`, `verbosity_subtests` | `int \| Literal["auto"]` |
| `tmp_path_retention_count` | `int \| str` (default is now `3`) |
| `log_level`, `log_cli_level`, `log_file_level` | `int \| str` |
| `log_auto_indent` | `int \| bool \| str` |
| `log_file_mode` | `Literal["w", "a"]` |
| `parametrize_long_str_id_strategy` | its `Literal` choices |

**How:** these options now use the `addini(type=...)` expressions from #14751 and #14791. `get_log_level_for_setting` now handles int levels directly. An int `0` (NOTSET) still counts as set, matching the old `"0"` string. The `int | bool | str` order for `log_auto_indent` keeps ini `"1"` meaning one space, not `True`.

**Compat note:** because union members are tried in order, `getini()` now returns `int` for ini-file values like `verbosity_assertions = 2` or `log_level = 10`, where it used to return a `str`. This is the same trade-off #14954 made for `max_warnings`. Callers in pytest already convert with `int()`. A third-party plugin that calls `getini()` on these options and expects a `str` would see the change.

**Docs:** the "must be quoted in TOML" notes are removed. The TOML `minversion = 3.0` example is now quoted, because a float is rejected there and would turn `8.10` into `8.1`. Copy-pasted `log_cli_level` lines in the `log_level` and `log_file_level` examples are fixed, and the `--help` dump is refreshed (it also had a stale `faulthandler_timeout`).

- [x] Allow maintainers to push and squash when merging my commits.
- [x] If AI agents were used, they are credited in `Co-authored-by` commit trailers.
- [x] Create a new changelog file in the `changelog` directory.

Native TOML numeric faulthandler_timeout is rejected

﻿## Summary

`faulthandler_timeout` rejects native numeric values in TOML configuration, even though the option is documented as a float and the TOML examples use a number.

## Reproduction

On pytest `main` at `f5240bef4`, with Python 3.12 on Windows:

```toml
[pytest]
faulthandler_timeout = 5
```

Running a test produces:

```text
ERROR: pytest.toml: config option 'faulthandler_timeout' expects a string, got int: 5
```

The same option works when configured through INI-style configuration or as a quoted TOML string.

## Expected behavior

Native TOML integers and floats should be accepted for this float-valued option, consistent with the documentation and the other typed TOML options.

I have a small local fix and regression test ready for review.

﻿Closes #15132

## Summary

`faulthandler_timeout` is documented as a float and supports native TOML configuration, but numeric TOML values were rejected because the option was registered without a type. Register it as `float | str` so native TOML numbers and existing string values are accepted.

The regression test covers integer, float, and quoted-string TOML values.

## Testing

- `uvx pre-commit run --files src/_pytest/faulthandler.py testing/test_faulthandler.py AUTHORS changelog/15132.bugfix.rst`

task:
Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` after a one-liner whose body starts with a name

### Description

`# fmt: skip` on a one-line compound statement with a semicolon-separated body crashes when the body starts with a bare name:

```python
if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

```console
$ black example.py
error: cannot format example.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.2.dev13+gc3c44ed79 on Python (CPython) 3.14.4 produced invalid code:
cannot parse: example.py:1:8
    if True:if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

The same happens for `while x: a; b`, `for i in r: i; print(i)`, `with a: b; c`, `def f(): x; return x` and `class A: x; y = 1` (26.10.1 too), while `if True: a(); b()` works.

For these one-liners the header is prepended to the skipped nodes (#4800). When the body starts with a bare leaf, the backward walk over the nodes on the line climbs from that leaf to the statement and keeps going, so it already collected the header, and the header was added a second time. This only prepends the header leaves the walk hasn't covered. Checking coverage by leaf matters for `def`, where the walk collects the parameters as one node but the header lists `(` and `)` as leaves.

The new case is `fmtskip_one_liner_bare_name.py`; it fails on `main` with the error above. The full test suite and the pre-commit hooks pass, and running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview) gives the same results as `main`.

Not part of this PR: a block whose only body statement is on its own line is taken for an expanded one-liner and printed as `if True:    a; b  # fmt: skip`, as `main` already does when the body is a call. That is the separate `_find_compound_statement_context` heuristic:

```python
if True:
    a; b  # fmt: skip
```

- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?

- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation? (Not needed.)

import re
from collections.abc import Collection, Iterator
from dataclasses import dataclass
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import Final, Union

from black.mode import Mode
from black.nodes import (
    CLOSING_BRACKETS,
    OPENING_BRACKETS,
    STANDALONE_COMMENT,
    STATEMENT,
    WHITESPACE,
    container_of,
    first_leaf_of,
    is_type_comment_string,
    last_leaf,
    make_simple_prefix,
    preceding_leaf,
    syms,
)
from blib2to3.pgen2 import token
from blib2to3.pytree import Leaf, Node

# types
LN = Union[Leaf, Node]

FMT_OFF: Final = {"# fmt: off", "# fmt:off", "# yapf: disable"}
FMT_SKIP: Final = {"# fmt: skip", "# fmt:skip"}
FMT_ON: Final = {"# fmt: on", "# fmt:on", "# yapf: enable"}

# Compound statements we care about for fmt: skip handling
# (excludes except_clause and case_block which aren't standalone compound statements)
_COMPOUND_STATEMENTS: Final = STATEMENT - {syms.except_clause, syms.case_block}

COMMENT_EXCEPTIONS = " !:#'"
_COMMENT_PREFIX = "# "
_COMMENT_LIST_SEPARATOR = ";"


@dataclass
class ProtoComment:
    """Describes a piece of syntax that is a comment.

    It's not a :class:`blib2to3.pytree.Leaf` so that:

    * it can be cached (`Leaf` objects should not be reused more than once as
      they store their lineno, column, prefix, and parent information);
    * `newlines` and `consumed` fields are kept separate from the `value`. This
      simplifies handling of special marker comments like ``# fmt: off/on``.
    """

    type: int  # token.COMMENT or STANDALONE_COMMENT
    value: str  # content of the comment
    newlines: int  # how many newlines before the comment
    consumed: int  # how many characters of the original leaf's prefix did we consume
    form_feed: bool  # is there a form feed before the comment
    leading_whitespace: str  # leading whitespace before the comment, if any
    original_value: str  # original comment text, before normalization
    prefix_line_index: int  # 0-based physical line index within the parsed prefix


def generate_comments(
    leaf: LN,
    mode: Mode,
    *,
    preserve_comment_formatting: bool = False,
    line_ranges_first_lineno: int = 0,
    line_ranges_selected: set[int] | None = None,
) -> Iterator[Leaf]:

    Comments in lib2to3 are shoved into the whitespace prefix.  This happens
    in `pgen2/driver.py:Driver.parse_tokens()`.  This was a brilliant implementation
    move because it does away with modifying the grammar to include all the
    possible places in which comments can be placed.

    The sad consequence for us though is that comments don't "belong" anywhere.
    This is why this function generates simple parentless Leaf objects for
    comments.  We simply don't know what the correct parent should be.

    No matter though, we can live without this.  We really only need to
    differentiate between inline and standalone comments.  The latter don't
    share the line with any code.

    Inline comments are emitted as regular token.COMMENT leaves.  Standalone
    are emitted with a fake STANDALONE_COMMENT token identifier.
    """
    total_consumed = 0

            line_ranges_selected is None or comment_lineno not in line_ranges_selected

Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` after a one-liner whose body starts with a name

### Description

`# fmt: skip` on a one-line compound statement with a semicolon-separated body crashes when the body starts with a bare name:

```python
if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

```console
$ black example.py
error: cannot format example.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.2.dev13+gc3c44ed79 on Python (CPython) 3.14.4 produced invalid code:
cannot parse: example.py:1:8
    if True:if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

The same happens for `while x: a; b`, `for i in r: i; print(i)`, `with a: b; c`, `def f(): x; return x` and `class A: x; y = 1` (26.10.1 too), while `if True: a(); b()` works.

For these one-liners the header is prepended to the skipped nodes (#4800). When the body starts with a bare leaf, the backward walk over the nodes on the line climbs from that leaf to the statement and keeps going, so it already collected the header, and the header was added a second time. This only prepends the header leaves the walk hasn't covered. Checking coverage by leaf matters for `def`, where the walk collects the parameters as one node but the header lists `(` and `)` as leaves.

The new case is `fmtskip_one_liner_bare_name.py`; it fails on `main` with the error above. The full test suite and the pre-commit hooks pass, and running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview) gives the same results as `main`.

Not part of this PR: a block whose only body statement is on its own line is taken for an expanded one-liner and printed as `if True:    a; b  # fmt: skip`, as `main` already does when the body is a call. That is the separate `_find_compound_statement_context` heuristic:

```python
if True:
    a; b  # fmt: skip
```

import re
from collections.abc import Collection, Iterator
from dataclasses import dataclass
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import Final, Union

from black.mode import Mode
from black.nodes import (
    CLOSING_BRACKETS,
    OPENING_BRACKETS,
    STANDALONE_COMMENT,
    STATEMENT,
    WHITESPACE,
    container_of,
    first_leaf_of,
    is_type_comment_string,
    last_leaf,
    make_simple_prefix,
    preceding_leaf,
    syms,
)
from blib2to3.pgen2 import token
from blib2to3.pytree import Leaf, Node

# types
LN = Union[Leaf, Node]

FMT_OFF: Final = {"# fmt: off", "# fmt:off", "# yapf: disable"}
FMT_SKIP: Final = {"# fmt: skip", "# fmt:skip"}
FMT_ON: Final = {"# fmt: on", "# fmt:on", "# yapf: enable"}

# Compound statements we care about for fmt: skip handling
# (excludes except_clause and case_block which aren't standalone compound statements)
_COMPOUND_STATEMENTS: Final = STATEMENT - {syms.except_clause, syms.case_block}

COMMENT_EXCEPTIONS = " !:#'"
_COMMENT_PREFIX = "# "
_COMMENT_LIST_SEPARATOR = ";"


@dataclass
class ProtoComment:
    """Describes a piece of syntax that is a comment.

    It's not a :class:`blib2to3.pytree.Leaf` so that:

    * it can be cached (`Leaf` objects should not be reused more than once as
      they store their lineno, column, prefix, and parent information);
    * `newlines` and `consumed` fields are kept separate from the `value`. This
      simplifies handling of special marker comments like ``# fmt: off/on``.
    """

    type: int  # token.COMMENT or STANDALONE_COMMENT
    value: str  # content of the comment
    newlines: int  # how many newlines before the comment
    consumed: int  # how many characters of the original leaf's prefix did we consume
    form_feed: bool  # is there a form feed before the comment
    leading_whitespace: str  # leading whitespace before the comment, if any
    original_value: str  # original comment text, before normalization
    prefix_line_index: int  # 0-based physical line index within the parsed prefix


def generate_comments(
    leaf: LN,
    mode: Mode,
    *,
    preserve_comment_formatting: bool = False,
    line_ranges_first_lineno: int = 0,
    line_ranges_selected: set[int] | None = None,
) -> Iterator[Leaf]:
    """Clean the prefix of the `leaf` and generate comments from it, if any.

    Comments in lib2to3 are shoved into the whitespace prefix.  This happens
    in `pgen2/driver.py:Driver.parse_tokens()`.  This was a brilliant implementation
    move because it does away with modifying the grammar to include all the
    possible places in which comments can be placed.

    The sad consequence for us though is that comments don't "belong" anywhere.
    This is why this function generates simple parentless Leaf objects for
    comments.  We simply don't know what the correct parent should be.

    No matter though, we can live without this.  We really only need to
    differentiate between inline and standalone comments.  The latter don't
    share the line with any code.

    Inline comments are emitted as regular token.COMMENT leaves.  Standalone
    are emitted with a fake STANDALONE_COMMENT token identifier.
    """
    total_consumed = 0
    comments = list_comments(
        leaf.prefix, is_endmarker=leaf.type == token.ENDMARKER, mode=mode
    )
    prefix_line_count = len(re.split(r"\r?\n|\r", leaf.prefix)) - 1
    for pc in comments:
        total_consumed = pc.consumed
        prefix = make_simple_prefix(pc.newlines, pc.form_feed)
        value = pc.value
        comment_lineno = (
            line_ranges_first_lineno - prefix_line_count + pc.prefix_line_index
        )
        should_preserve = preserve_comment_formatting and (
            line_ranges_selected is None or comment_lineno not in line_ranges_selected
        )
        if should_preserve:
            value = pc.leading_whitespace + pc.original_value
        yield Leaf(pc.type, value, prefix=prefix)
    normalize_trailing_prefix(leaf, total_consumed)

Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` after a one-liner whose body starts with a name

### Description

`# fmt: skip` on a one-line compound statement with a semicolon-separated body crashes when the body starts with a bare name:

```python
if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

```console
$ black example.py
error: cannot format example.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.2.dev13+gc3c44ed79 on Python (CPython) 3.14.4 produced invalid code:
cannot parse: example.py:1:8
    if True:if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

The same happens for `while x: a; b`, `for i in r: i; print(i)`, `with a: b; c`, `def f(): x; return x` and `class A: x; y = 1` (26.10.1 too), while `if True: a(); b()` works.

For these one-liners the header is prepended to the skipped nodes (#4800). When the body starts with a bare leaf, the backward walk over the nodes on the line climbs from that leaf to the statement and keeps going, so it already collected the header, and the header was added a second time. This only prepends the header leaves the walk hasn't covered. Checking coverage by leaf matters for `def`, where the walk collects the parameters as one node but the header lists `(` and `)` as leaves.

The new case is `fmtskip_one_liner_bare_name.py`; it fails on `main` with the error above. The full test suite and the pre-commit hooks pass, and running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview) gives the same results as `main`.

Not part of this PR: a block whose only body statement is on its own line is taken for an expanded one-liner and printed as `if True:    a; b  # fmt: skip`, as `main` already does when the body is a call. That is the separate `_find_compound_statement_context` heuristic:

```python
if True:
    a; b  # fmt: skip
```

FMT_SKIP: Final = {"# fmt: skip", "# fmt:skip"}
FMT_ON: Final = {"# fmt: on", "# fmt:on", "# yapf: enable"}

# (excludes except_clause and case_block which aren't standalone compound statements)

_COMMENT_PREFIX = "# "
_COMMENT_LIST_SEPARATOR = ";"


@dataclass
class ProtoComment:
    """Describes a piece of syntax that is a comment.

    It's not a :class:`blib2to3.pytree.Leaf` so that:

    * it can be cached (`Leaf` objects should not be reused more than once as
      they store their lineno, column, prefix, and parent information);
    * `newlines` and `consumed` fields are kept separate from the `value`. This
      simplifies handling of special marker comments like ``# fmt: off/on``.
    """

    type: int  # token.COMMENT or STANDALONE_COMMENT
    value: str  # content of the comment
    newlines: int  # how many newlines before the comment
    consumed: int  # how many characters of the original leaf's prefix did we consume
    form_feed: bool  # is there a form feed before the comment
    leading_whitespace: str  # leading whitespace before the comment, if any
    original_value: str  # original comment text, before normalization
    prefix_line_index: int  # 0-based physical line index within the parsed prefix

    leaf: LN,
    mode: Mode,

    preserve_comment_formatting: bool = False,
    line_ranges_first_lineno: int = 0,
    line_ranges_selected: set[int] | None = None,

    Comments in lib2to3 are shoved into the whitespace prefix.  This happens
    in `pgen2/driver.py:Driver.parse_tokens()`.  This was a brilliant implementation
    move because it does away with modifying the grammar to include all the
    possible places in which comments can be placed.

    The sad consequence for us though is that comments don't "belong" anywhere.
    This is why this function generates simple parentless Leaf objects for
    comments.  We simply don't know what the correct parent should be.

    No matter though, we can live without this.  We really only need to
    differentiate between inline and standalone comments.  The latter don't
    share the line with any code.

    are emitted with a fake STANDALONE_COMMENT token identifier.

        leaf.prefix, is_endmarker=leaf.type == token.ENDMARKER, mode=mode
    )

        total_consumed = pc.consumed
        prefix = make_simple_prefix(pc.newlines, pc.form_feed)
        value = pc.value
        comment_lineno = (
            line_ranges_first_lineno - prefix_line_count + pc.prefix_line_index
        )
        should_preserve = preserve_comment_formatting and (
            line_ranges_selected is None or comment_lineno not in line_ranges_selected
        )

            value = pc.leading_whitespace + pc.original_value

task:
Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` after a one-liner whose body starts with a name

### Description

`# fmt: skip` on a one-line compound statement with a semicolon-separated body crashes when the body starts with a bare name:

```python
if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

```console
$ black example.py
error: cannot format example.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.2.dev13+gc3c44ed79 on Python (CPython) 3.14.4 produced invalid code:
cannot parse: example.py:1:8
    if True:if True: a; b  # fmt: skip
```

The same happens for `while x: a; b`, `for i in r: i; print(i)`, `with a: b; c`, `def f(): x; return x` and `class A: x; y = 1` (26.10.1 too), while `if True: a(); b()` works.

For these one-liners the header is prepended to the skipped nodes (#4800). When the body starts with a bare leaf, the backward walk over the nodes on the line climbs from that leaf to the statement and keeps going, so it already collected the header, and the header was added a second time. This only prepends the header leaves the walk hasn't covered. Checking coverage by leaf matters for `def`, where the walk collects the parameters as one node but the header lists `(` and `)` as leaves.

The new case is `fmtskip_one_liner_bare_name.py`; it fails on `main` with the error above. The full test suite and the pre-commit hooks pass, and running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview) gives the same results as `main`.

Not part of this PR: a block whose only body statement is on its own line is taken for an expanded one-liner and printed as `if True:    a; b  # fmt: skip`, as `main` already does when the body is a call. That is the separate `_find_compound_statement_context` heuristic:

```python
if True:
    a; b  # fmt: skip
```

task:
blackd: keep the skipped first line inside the returned diff

### Description

`blackd` computes the response patch in `format_code()`, but the first line that was
skipped for `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` was re-attached to the formatted output afterwards
in `handle()`. With `X-Diff: true` and `X-Skip-Source-First-Line: true` combined, the
response body was therefore a raw source line pasted in front of a unified diff of only
the remaining text:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python
In	2026-10-21 12:00:00.000000+00:00
Out	2026-10-21 12:00:00.100000+00:00
@@ -1 +1 @@
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

That is not a valid patch — the leading `#!/usr/bin/env python` is neither a diff header
nor a hunk body, so `patch`/`git apply` reject it, and the returned line numbers describe
the request with its first line removed.

Moving the `header` into `format_code()` and restoring it before `only_diff` is handled
puts the skipped line into both sides of the diff, so it shows up as context and the hunks
describe the whole request body:

```
--- [Deterministic header]
+++ [Deterministic header]
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env python
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

Behaviour for the existing combinations is unchanged: `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` without
`X-Diff` still returns the skipped line followed by the formatted source (the assertion in
`test_blackd_skip_first_source_line` still passes), and `X-Diff` alone is untouched since
`header` is then the empty string. `req_str = header + req_str` in `handle()` was dead
code — the local rebinding was never read again — so it is removed along with the
post-hoc concatenation.

No existing issue; I found this while reading the handler. The changelog entry uses the
number this PR is expected to get (#5573); happy to adjust if it lands differently.

### Checklist - did you ...

- [x] Implement any code style changes under the `--preview` style, following the stability policy? (N/A — no formatting behaviour change, this is a `blackd` response bugfix)
- [x] Add an entry in `CHANGES.md` if necessary?
- [x] Add / update tests if necessary?
- [x] Add new / update outdated documentation? (N/A — the documented header semantics are unchanged)

### Verification

- New `test_blackd_skip_first_source_line_with_diff` fails against `origin/main`
  (`287d5709`) with `#!/usr/bin/env python\n--- [Deterministic header]...` vs the expected
  patch, and passes with this change.
- `pytest tests/test_blackd.py -q` → 40 passed.
- `pytest tests/ -k blackd -q` → 40 passed, 1 skipped, 557 deselected.
- `black --check --diff src/blackd/__init__.py tests/test_blackd.py` → 2 files left
  unchanged; `CHANGES.md` lines stay within the file's wrap width.

Note: I could not run the repository's `pre-commit`/`tox -e lint` suite in this
environment (no `flake8`/`mypy` available, and the compiled `prp` extension is not
installed, so only the `blackd` test modules were exercised). CI will cover the rest.

blackd: keep the skipped first line inside the returned diff

### Description

`blackd` computes the response patch in `format_code()`, but the first line that was
skipped for `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` was re-attached to the formatted output afterwards
in `handle()`. With `X-Diff: true` and `X-Skip-Source-First-Line: true` combined, the
response body was therefore a raw source line pasted in front of a unified diff of only
the remaining text:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python
In	2026-10-21 12:00:00.000000+00:00
Out	2026-10-21 12:00:00.100000+00:00
@@ -1 +1 @@
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

That is not a valid patch — the leading `#!/usr/bin/env python` is neither a diff header
nor a hunk body, so `patch`/`git apply` reject it, and the returned line numbers describe
the request with its first line removed.

Moving the `header` into `format_code()` and restoring it before `only_diff` is handled
puts the skipped line into both sides of the diff, so it shows up as context and the hunks
describe the whole request body:

```
--- [Deterministic header]
+++ [Deterministic header]
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env python
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

Behaviour for the existing combinations is unchanged: `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` without
`X-Diff` still returns the skipped line followed by the formatted source (the assertion in
`test_blackd_skip_first_source_line` still passes), and `X-Diff` alone is untouched since
`header` is then the empty string. `req_str = header + req_str` in `handle()` was dead
code — the local rebinding was never read again — so it is removed along with the
post-hoc concatenation.

No existing issue; I found this while reading the handler. The changelog entry uses the
number this PR is expected to get (#5573); happy to adjust if it lands differently.

    SKIP_SOURCE_FIRST_LINE,
    SKIP_STRING_NORMALIZATION_HEADER,
    SKIP_MAGIC_TRAILING_COMMA,
    PREVIEW,
    UNSTABLE,
    ENABLE_UNSTABLE_FEATURE,
    FAST_OR_SAFE_HEADER,
    DIFF_HEADER,

    pass

blackd: keep the skipped first line inside the returned diff

### Description

`blackd` computes the response patch in `format_code()`, but the first line that was
skipped for `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` was re-attached to the formatted output afterwards
in `handle()`. With `X-Diff: true` and `X-Skip-Source-First-Line: true` combined, the
response body was therefore a raw source line pasted in front of a unified diff of only
the remaining text:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python
In	2026-10-21 12:00:00.000000+00:00
Out	2026-10-21 12:00:00.100000+00:00
@@ -1 +1 @@
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

That is not a valid patch — the leading `#!/usr/bin/env python` is neither a diff header
nor a hunk body, so `patch`/`git apply` reject it, and the returned line numbers describe
the request with its first line removed.

Moving the `header` into `format_code()` and restoring it before `only_diff` is handled
puts the skipped line into both sides of the diff, so it shows up as context and the hunks
describe the whole request body:

```
--- [Deterministic header]
+++ [Deterministic header]
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env python
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

Behaviour for the existing combinations is unchanged: `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` without
`X-Diff` still returns the skipped line followed by the formatted source (the assertion in
`test_blackd_skip_first_source_line` still passes), and `X-Diff` alone is untouched since
`header` is then the empty string. `req_str = header + req_str` in `handle()` was dead
code — the local rebinding was never read again — so it is removed along with the
post-hoc concatenation.

No existing issue; I found this while reading the handler. The changelog entry uses the
number this PR is expected to get (#5573); happy to adjust if it lands differently.

import asyncio
import logging
import os
from concurrent.futures import Executor, ProcessPoolExecutor
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from functools import cache, partial
from multiprocessing import freeze_support

try:
    from aiohttp import web
    from multidict import MultiMapping

    from .middlewares import cors
except ImportError as ie:
    raise ImportError(
        f"aiohttp dependency is not installed: {ie}. "
        + "Please re-install black with the '[d]' extra install "
        + "to obtain aiohttp: `pip install black[d]`"
    ) from None

import click

import black
from _black_version import version as __version__
from black.concurrency import maybe_use_uvloop

# This is used internally by tests to shut down the server prematurely
_stop_signal = asyncio.Event()

# Request headers
PROTOCOL_VERSION_HEADER = "X-Protocol-Version"
LINE_LENGTH_HEADER = "X-Line-Length"
PYTHON_VARIANT_HEADER = "X-Python-Variant"
SKIP_SOURCE_FIRST_LINE = "X-Skip-Source-First-Line"
SKIP_STRING_NORMALIZATION_HEADER = "X-Skip-String-Normalization"
SKIP_MAGIC_TRAILING_COMMA = "X-Skip-Magic-Trailing-Comma"
PREVIEW = "X-Preview"
UNSTABLE = "X-Unstable"
ENABLE_UNSTABLE_FEATURE = "X-Enable-Unstable-Feature"
FAST_OR_SAFE_HEADER = "X-Fast-Or-Safe"
DIFF_HEADER = "X-Diff"

BLACK_HEADERS = [
    PROTOCOL_VERSION_HEADER,
    LINE_LENGTH_HEADER,
    PYTHON_VARIANT_HEADER,
    SKIP_SOURCE_FIRST_LINE,
    SKIP_STRING_NORMALIZATION_HEADER,
    SKIP_MAGIC_TRAILING_COMMA,
    PREVIEW,
    UNSTABLE,
    ENABLE_UNSTABLE_FEATURE,
    FAST_OR_SAFE_HEADER,
    DIFF_HEADER,
]

# Response headers
BLACK_VERSION_HEADER = "X-Black-Version"
DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_SIZE = 5 * 1024 * 1024
DEFAULT_WORKERS = os.cpu_count() or 1


class HeaderError(Exception):
    pass


class InvalidVariantHeader(Exception):
    pass


@click.command(context_settings={"help_option_names": ["-h", "--help"]})
@click.option(
    "--bind-host",
    type=str,
    help="Address to bind the server to.",
    default="localhost",
    show_default=True,
)
@click.option(
    "--bind-port", type=int, help="Port to listen on", default=45484, show_default=True
)
@click.option(
    "--cors-allow-origin",
    "cors_allow_origins",
    multiple=True,
    help="Origin allowed to access blackd over CORS. Can be passed multiple times.",
)
@click.option(
    "--max-body-size",
    type=click.IntRange(min=1),
    default=DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_SIZE,
    show_default=True,
    help="Maximum request body size in bytes.",
)
@click.version_option(version=black.__version__)
def main(
    bind_host: str,
    bind_port: int,
    cors_allow_origins: tuple[str, ...],
    max_body_size: int,
) -> None:
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    app = make_app(cors_allow_origins=cors_allow_origins, max_body_size=max_body_size)
    ver = black.__version__
    black.out(f"blackd version {ver} listening on {bind_host} port {bind_port}")
    loop = maybe_use_uvloop()
    try:
        web.run_app(
            app,
            host=bind_host,
            port=bind_port,
            handle_signals=True,
            print=None,
            loop=loop,
        )
    finally:
        if not loop.is_closed():
            loop.close()


@cache
def executor() -> Executor:
    return ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=DEFAULT_WORKERS)


def make_app(
    *,
    cors_allow_origins: tuple[str, ...] = (),
    max_body_size: int = DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_SIZE,
) -> web.Application:
    app = web.Application(
        client_max_size=max_body_size,
        middlewares=[
            cors(
                allow_headers=(*BLACK_HEADERS, "Content-Type"),
                allow_origins=frozenset(cors_allow_origins),
                expose_headers=(BLACK_VERSION_HEADER,),
            )
        ],
    )
    app.add_routes([
        web.post(
            "/",
            partial(
                handle,
                executor=executor(),
                executor_semaphore=asyncio.BoundedSemaphore(DEFAULT_WORKERS),
            ),
        )
    ])
    return

blackd: keep the skipped first line inside the returned diff

### Description

`blackd` computes the response patch in `format_code()`, but the first line that was
skipped for `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` was re-attached to the formatted output afterwards
in `handle()`. With `X-Diff: true` and `X-Skip-Source-First-Line: true` combined, the
response body was therefore a raw source line pasted in front of a unified diff of only
the remaining text:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python
In	2026-10-21 12:00:00.000000+00:00
Out	2026-10-21 12:00:00.100000+00:00
@@ -1 +1 @@
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

That is not a valid patch — the leading `#!/usr/bin/env python` is neither a diff header
nor a hunk body, so `patch`/`git apply` reject it, and the returned line numbers describe
the request with its first line removed.

Moving the `header` into `format_code()` and restoring it before `only_diff` is handled
puts the skipped line into both sides of the diff, so it shows up as context and the hunks
describe the whole request body:

```
--- [Deterministic header]
+++ [Deterministic header]
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env python
-i = [1,2,3]
+i = [1, 2, 3]
```

Behaviour for the existing combinations is unchanged: `X-Skip-Source-First-Line` without
`X-Diff` still returns the skipped line followed by the formatted source (the assertion in
`test_blackd_skip_first_source_line` still passes), and `X-Diff` alone is untouched since
`header` is then the empty string. `req_str = header + req_str` in `handle()` was dead
code — the local rebinding was never read again — so it is removed along with the
post-hoc concatenation.

No existing issue; I found this while reading the handler. The changelog entry uses the
number this PR is expected to get (#5573); happy to adjust if it lands differently.

Fix lambda turned into a tuple by a comment before its parameters

### Description

A standalone comment between `lambda` and its parameters makes Black turn a parenthesized lambda into a tuple:

```python
f = (
    lambda  # comment 1
    # comment 2
    *args, **kwargs: # comment 3
    aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa(*args, **kwargs) + 1
)
```

In safe mode this fails with "produced code that is not equivalent to the source". With `--fast` the output is:

```python
f = (
    lambda  # comment 1
    # comment 2
    *args,
    **kwargs: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa(  # comment 3
        *args, **kwargs
    ),
    +1,
)
```

which is a tuple. 26.10.1 behaves the same.

The standalone comment starts a new line that holds the parameters but not `lambda`, so the bracket tracker never sees the `lambda` that normally hides the parameter commas, and `delimiter_split` splits at them as if they were tuple elements (and then adds a trailing comma). This is close to #5533, where a comment inside a parameter default caused the same tuple, but here the comma that gets split is the parameter separator itself. Like the for-target commas in `is_split_after_delimiter` (#4296), commas whose parent is the `varargslist` of a lambda are now never delimiters.

I found this by running Black over the CPython 3.14 standard library and Ruff's formatter fixtures (2,202 files, stable and preview): Ruff's `expression/lambda.py` failed in both styles and now formats, with no new failures in the run.

### Description

A standalone comment between `lambda` and its parameters makes Black turn a parenthesized lambda into a tuple:

```python
f = (
    lambda  # comment 1

    *args, **kwargs: # comment 3
    aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa(*args, **kwargs) + 1
)
```

In safe mode this fails with "produced code that is not equivalent to the source". With `--fast` the output is:

```python
f = (
    lambda  # comment 1
    # comment 2
    *args,
    **kwargs: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa(  # comment 3
        *args, **kwargs
    ),
    +1,
)
```

The standalone comment starts a new line that holds the parameters but not `lambda`, so the bracket tracker never sees the `lambda` that normally hides the parameter commas, and `delimiter_split` splits at them as if they were tuple elements (and then adds a trailing comma). task:
Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` on a bracket followed by `if`/`else`

### Description

`# fmt: skip` on an opening bracket crashes Black when a conditional expression continues after the closing bracket:

```python
x = (  # fmt: skip
    a
) if condition else b
```

fails with "INTERNAL ERROR: Black produced invalid code: cannot parse: 4:4". The same happens with `[  # fmt: skip`, with `a if (  # fmt: skip` ... `) else c`, and after `return`, `lambda:` or in a `while` header. 26.5.1 crashes on these too.

The skipped line hides everything up to the closing bracket, including the first operand of the conditional, so the `test` node that's left starts at `if` (or `else`). `visit_test` still wraps it in invisible parentheses, and the right-hand split then makes them visible right after the hidden code:

```python
x = (  # fmt: skip
    a
) (
    if condition else b
)
```

This doesn't reach the `_force_standalone_comment_split` path from #5538, because the split succeeds first. Outside of brackets these parentheses are now left out, so the rest of the expression stays on the closing bracket's line, like `+ [3]` does after #5538. Inside brackets they're kept, so existing output there doesn't change.

A conditional inside brackets that's too long to fit on one line still crashes the same way, since it gets split onto its own line before the parentheses are made visible. That needs a different fix, so I left it out.

task:
Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` on a bracket followed by `if`/`else`

### Description

`# fmt: skip` on an opening bracket crashes Black when a conditional expression continues after the closing bracket:

```python
x = (  # fmt: skip
    a
) if condition else b
```

fails with "INTERNAL ERROR: Black produced invalid code: cannot parse: 4:4". The same happens with `[  # fmt: skip`, with `a if (  # fmt: skip` ... `) else c`, and after `return`, `lambda:` or in a `while` header. 26.5.1 crashes on these too.

The skipped line hides everything up to the closing bracket, including the first operand of the conditional, so the `test` node that's left starts at `if` (or `else`). `visit_test` still wraps it in invisible parentheses, and the right-hand split then makes them visible right after the hidden code:

```python
x = (  # fmt: skip
    a
) (
    if condition else b
)
```

This doesn't reach the `_force_standalone_comment_split` path from #5538, because the split succeeds first. Outside of brackets these parentheses are now left out, so the rest of the expression stays on the closing bracket's line, like `+ [3]` does after #5538. Inside brackets they're kept, so existing output there doesn't change.

A conditional inside brackets that's too long to fit on one line still crashes the same way, since it gets split onto its own line before the parentheses are made visible. That needs a different fix, so I left it out.

task:
Fix crash on `# fmt: skip` on a bracket followed by `if`/`else`

### Description

`# fmt: skip` on an opening bracket crashes Black when a conditional expression continues after the closing bracket:

```python
x = (  # fmt: skip
    a
) if condition else b
```

fails with "INTERNAL ERROR: Black produced invalid code: cannot parse: 4:4". The same happens with `[  # fmt: skip`, with `a if (  # fmt: skip` ... `) else c`, and after `return`, `lambda:` or in a `while` header. 26.5.1 crashes on these too.

The skipped line hides everything up to the closing bracket, including the first operand of the conditional, so the `test` node that's left starts at `if` (or `else`). `visit_test` still wraps it in invisible parentheses, and the right-hand split then makes them visible right after the hidden code:

```python
x = (  # fmt: skip
    a
) (
    if condition else b
)
```

This doesn't reach the `_force_standalone_comment_split` path from #5538, because the split succeeds first. Outside of brackets these parentheses are now left out, so the rest of the expression stays on the closing bracket's line, like `+ [3]` does after #5538. Inside brackets they're kept, so existing output there doesn't change.

A conditional inside brackets that's too long to fit on one line still crashes the same way, since it gets split onto its own line before the parentheses are made visible. That needs a different fix, so I left it out.

Fix headers swallowed by comment-only fmt: off blocks

<!-- Hello! Thanks for submitting a PR. To help make things go a bit smoother
     we would appreciate that you go through this template. -->

### Description

A `# fmt: off` / `# fmt: on` block that only holds comments has no newline at the
end. When the next line is a compound statement header with `# fmt: skip`, Black
puts the header on the same line as `# fmt: on`, so it turns into part of the
comment.

Input:

```python
def setup():
    connect()


# fmt: off
# fmt: on
if DEBUG :  # fmt: skip
    enable_tracing()
```

`black --fast` exits with 0 and writes:

```python
def setup():
    connect()


    # fmt: off
# fmt: onif DEBUG :  # fmt: skip
    enable_tracing()
```

The `if` is gone and `enable_tracing()` is now inside `setup()`. Without `--fast`,
Black fails with an internal error instead. The same thing happens with
`--line-ranges` when the header is outside the selected lines, even without
`# fmt: skip`.

The `# fmt: skip` case started in 26.10.0 with #5401. The `--line-ranges` case is
older, it also happens on 26.5.1.

The fix adds the missing newline in the two places that join this block with the
code after it, one in `comments.py` and one in `ranges.py`. I added tests for `if`,
`elif`, `else`, `while`, `with`, `finally`, `def`, `class` and `case` headers.

#5525 fixes a different spot in `ranges.py` for the same kind of block (simple
statements and decorators). The two PRs don't overlap.
